walkthrough.title: Code & Hardware Walkthrough
walkthrough.description: Scroll down to inspect each section of the C code. The hardware components on the left highlight in sync with the relevant code block on screen.

explanation.title: What does this section do?
paragraphs: Before the microcontroller starts, configuration bits define how the hardware behaves. The `#pragma config` lines set the oscillator mode (HS — High Speed), watchdog timer (WDTE), and power-up timer (PWRTE).

Pin definitions make the rest of the code readable by using meaningful names like `RS`, `EN`, and `D4`. The LCD is driven through PORTD and PORTC, while buttons are read from PORTB (RB0–RB3). This creates a direct mapping between software and hardware.
bullets: HS mode allows high-speed operation with a 20 MHz crystal.
WDTE = OFF prevents the device from resetting itself automatically.
Buttons are set as inputs with `TRISB = 0x0F`; LCD pins are outputs with `TRISD = 0x00`.

explanation.title: How does the LCD work?
paragraphs: The LCD operates in 4-bit mode. Instead of 8 data lines, only D4–D7 are used, saving pins on the PIC. Every command or character is sent in two halves: the high nibble first, then the low nibble.

The `Lcd_Hazirla()` function sends the required initialization sequence (0x30, 0x20, 0x28, 0x0C, 0x06, 0x01). `0x28` selects 4-bit mode and 2 lines, `0x0C` turns the display on with no cursor, and `0x01` clears the screen. `Lcd_Git()` positions the cursor at a specific row and column.
bullets: 4-bit mode splits data into two nibbles, saving I/O pins.
RS = 0 sends a command; RS = 1 sends data (a character).
A short pulse on the EN pin tells the LCD to latch the command.
A 2 ms delay after each command gives the LCD time to process.

explanation.title: How does Timer1 keep time?
paragraphs: With a 20 MHz crystal and a 1:8 prescaler, Timer1 overflows approximately every 50 milliseconds. The interrupt service routine (`__interrupt`) fires on each overflow and increments a counter variable called `kesme_sayaci`.

When the counter reaches 20 (20 × 50 ms = 1000 ms = 1 second), a full second has elapsed. At this point the seconds variable is incremented; when it passes 60, minutes roll over; when minutes pass 60, hours roll over. When hours reach 24 they reset to 0. All of this rollover logic runs automatically inside the interrupt.
bullets: TMR1H = 0x86 and TMR1L = 0x02 are pre-calculated preload values for a 50 ms overflow.
TMR1IF = 0 clears the interrupt flag so the next overflow can be detected.
GIE = 1 (Global Interrupt Enable) turns interrupts on.
The ISR runs independently of the main loop, so the clock updates in the background.

explanation.title: What are buttons and debounce?
paragraphs: Mechanical buttons bounce briefly when pressed, generating multiple 'pressed' signals. To avoid unwanted repeated actions, we use rising-edge detection: the code reacts only when the signal transitions from 0 to 1.

Variables like `b1_eski` and `b2_eski` store the previous button state. The condition `if (B_SAAT_ARTIR == 1 && b1_eski == 0)` fires exactly once per press, because it requires the previous state to be 0 and the current state to be 1. Holding the button down will not increment the value again.
bullets: Debounce prevents false readings caused by mechanical switch bounce.
Rising edge: captures the exact moment the signal goes from 0 to 1.
Hour decrement checks the 0 boundary; decrementing below 0 wraps to 23.
Minute increment/decrement also updates the hour value on rollover.
